summary: This standards-track memo specifies the core of the OPES Callout Protocol (OCP). An OPES intermediary uses it to send application messages to a callout server, which adapts them and sends them back. OCP carries messages from other protocols and is designed to be independent of any one application.

eli5.summary: A helper in the middle of a message's journey can hand it to a specialist, who changes it, such as translating it, and hands it back. This protocol defines how they talk.

questions: what is the opes callout protocol
how do opes intermediaries talk to callout servers
what is data preservation in ocp
subtitle: How an intermediary hands messages to a specialist server for adaptation and gets the result back.

tldr.problem: An OPES processor sitting between a data provider and a data consumer needs a standard way to delegate adaptation work, such as virus scanning or translation, to callout servers.
tldr.mechanism: OCP is a text-based protocol over a reliable, order-preserving transport. The processor opens a connection and a transaction, streams the original application message in Data Use Mine messages, and the callout server streams the adapted message back.
tldr.outcome: The core is application-agnostic, with negotiation, data-preservation and early-termination optimizations. HTTP and other application specifics are left to separate profiles.

facts.label: Core overhead
facts.value: About 100 - 200 octets per small application message

today: RFC 4037 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines only the application-agnostic core, so it relies on separate application profiles and extensions, such as the one for HTTP, for real adaptation of specific protocols.

sections.title: Where OCP Fits
sections.content:
The Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) architecture allows cooperative application services between a data provider, a data consumer and zero or more OPES processors. These services analyze and possibly transform application-level messages. A processor can delegate the work to callout servers, and it talks to them using the OPES Callout Protocol (OCP). RFC 4037 specifies only the core of that protocol.

The core is application-agnostic. A separate series of documents covers application-specific aspects. For example, a separate draft on HTTP adaptation describes how HTTP messages and meta-information travel over OCP. Within the core's scope is communication between a single OPES processor and a single callout server.

The RFC deliberately does not define the relationship between messages the processor proxies and messages it sends over OCP. A processor may pre-process or post-process messages, iterate over several callout servers, and choose which messages to send at all. Section 1.2 maps the other OPES documents, including use cases, the architecture, policy, security threats and IAB considerations.
sections.eli5: The clerk and the specialist only need to agree on how to pass things back and forth. What the specialist does to the letter, and which letters the clerk sends, are not part of these rules.

sections.title: Connections, Transactions and Dataflows
sections.content:
After a transport connection is up (usually TCP/IP, though no default port is assigned), both agents exchange Connection Start (CS) messages. They can then negotiate features before exchanging application messages. A connection may carry multiple concurrent transactions, but it carries at most one OCP message at a time.

To adapt a message, the processor sends TS (Transaction Start), then AMS (Application Message Start), then data in DUM messages. This is the original dataflow. The server usually answers with its own AMS and sends the adapted dataflow the same way. Each side closes its message with AME, and a TE ends the transaction, which can be sent by either side. The two flows may overlap in time.

In the core, a transaction deals with a single original and a single adapted application message. Either side can end a message, transaction or connection early, and the termination message includes a result. OCP Core defines no messages for stalled peers, so an agent MUST forcefully terminate any connection, negotiation or transaction that is not making progress. A Progress Query (PQ) can be used first. The RFC puts the overhead at about 100 - 200 octets per small application message.
sections.eli5: The clerk says a new job is starting, hands over the letter in pieces, and says the job is finished. The specialist hands back the changed letter in pieces too, even while the clerk is still talking.

sections.title: Message Format and Result Codes
sections.content:
An OCP message is a name, then optional parameters, then an optional payload, ending in ; and a CRLF. The ABNF has three kinds of value: atoms, lists in parentheses and structures in braces, which can nest. Parameters can be anonymous (positional) or named. Names are case sensitive, there is no implied linear whitespace rule, and UTF-8 is the default encoding.

Data is carried as a quoted value: a decimal size, a colon, then exactly that many octets. Sizes cannot exceed 2147483647 and cannot have leading zeros. Any bare value can be sent as a quoted value with the same meaning, so 1234 and "4:1234" are equivalent. This makes it possible to carry arbitrary bytes safely.

Many messages end with a result, a structure holding a numeric status code and an optional reason phrase. The core defines three codes: 200 (OK), 206 (partial, used on AME when a dataflow ended early) and 400 (failure). A recipient of an unknown code MUST act as if it received 400, and one that finds no result MUST act as if it received 200. A message that breaks the rules is invalid: the agent MUST end the transaction, or the connection if the scope is unclear, using status 400.
sections.eli5: Every note starts with a short name and ends with a semicolon. If you are sending something with odd letters in it, you first say how many characters it has, so the reader knows exactly where to stop.

sections.title: Negotiation of Features
sections.content:
Negotiation lets the agents agree on optional behavior, such as transport encryption, a data format or support for a new message. There are two primitives. A Negotiation Offer (NO) lists features, preferred first, and the responder picks at most one. A Negotiation Response (NR) carries the choice. If the answer is positive, the feature takes effect immediately. If it is negative, nothing changes, and further offers may follow.

Agents MUST NOT make, and MUST reject, offers that conflict with features already negotiated. The RFC's example is offering an HTTP profile on a connection with an SMTP profile already enabled. Either agent may make an offer, so concurrent offers could deadlock. The rules give the OPES processor priority, so only one offer per connection is honored at a time.

A Negotiation Phase is a stretch in which only a small set of messages may be sent, including NO, NR, AQ, AA, PQ, PA, PR and CE. The processor MUST send an offer immediately after CS, with an empty list if it has nothing to offer. A true Offer-Pending parameter keeps the phase open. An optional SG parameter limits negotiated features to one service group. Negotiated features apply to new transactions, not pending ones.
sections.eli5: Before the work begins, the two sides agree on extras, like whether to use a secret code. One side proposes options, the other picks one or says no thanks, and they never both speak at the same moment.

sections.title: Data Preservation and Early Termination
sections.content:
Many adaptations change little or nothing, so sending unchanged data to the server and back wastes effort. With data preservation, the processor announces in a Kept parameter of a DUM message that it will keep a contiguous chunk of the original data, described by an offset and size. The server can then send DUY (Data Use Yours), which has no payload, to say that the processor should use that chunk as if it came from the server. The processor MUST keep the chunk until the transaction ends unless the server says it is not needed, which the server does with DPI (Data Preservation Interest). The server can also add an As-is parameter on data it sends back unchanged, and a Modp parameter giving a prediction of how likely modification is.

For early termination, a server that no longer needs original data sends DWSR (Want Stop Receiving Data), and the processor SHOULD end the original flow with an AME carrying 206. A server that wants to stop sending adapted data sends DWSS and waits for the processor's DSS (Stop Sending Data), then ends with AME 206. The processor must be able to rebuild the full message from original data.

To get out of the loop entirely, the order matters: adapted flow first, then original flow. If the original flow ends first, the processor cannot reconstruct the rest, since only the callout service knows how original octets map to adapted ones. A server can send DWSS immediately followed by DWSR. The pause messages DWP, DPM and DWM let either side throttle data.
sections.eli5: If the specialist only changes one word, the clerk can keep the rest of the letter. The specialist says to use that part of the original, and nothing has to be sent twice.

sections.title: Type Declarations and Extending the Core
sections.content:
The RFC defines a small declaration language called the Protocol Element Type Declaration Mnemonic (PETDM). Every OCP Core parameter and message type is written with it, and extensions SHOULD do the same. New types extend base types, so a type such as xid is declared as extending uni, a unique numeric identifier in the range 0 to 2147483647. Dataflow-specific variants use the prefixes org-, adp-, my- and your-.

Extensions are the way to add features such as new application profiles or transport encryption. Recipients MUST ignore any valid but unknown name, parameter, member or payload, so extra information does not break older agents. Extensions MUST NOT change the core message format. They may change normative core behavior, but SHOULD NOT, and MUST require that any change be negotiated first. For features, the IANA maintains a registry of URIs. This specification defines none, and the standards-track prefix it suggests is http://www.iana.org/assignments/opes/ocp/.
sections.eli5: New rules can be added on top as long as they are announced first. Anyone who does not understand an extra note just ignores it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
OCP relays application messages that may contain sensitive information. Transport encryption can be negotiated, but agents may support unencrypted transport by default, and then messages are exposed to third-party recording and modification. The core does not require encryption or authentication, and expects OCP to be used partly in closed environments where trust is set up outside the protocol.

The RFC warns that implementation bugs, such as a buffer overflow caused by a malicious OPES processor, may expose data from other connections. Implementations should not assume identifiers are unique across all agents, and MUST check that an identifier is local to the connection before using it.

OCP is stateful, so resource exhaustion is a risk. The RFC lists places with no upper limit in the core: nesting depth and length of message elements, concurrent connections, service groups, concurrent transactions and concurrent adapted flows.
sections.eli5: The letters being passed around might be private, and the core does not lock the line by default. Both helpers also need to make sure nobody can overload them or trick them with fake ticket numbers.

items.label: Connection Start
items.desc: First message on a connection, sent exactly once.

items.label: Connection End
items.desc: Ends the connection.

items.label: Service Group Created
items.desc: Associates a list of services with a group id.

items.label: Service Group Destroyed
items.desc: Forgets a service group.

items.label: Transaction Start
items.desc: Sent by the processor to begin a transaction.

items.label: Transaction End
items.desc: Ends a transaction.

items.label: Application Message Start
items.desc: Starts an original or adapted message.

items.label: Application Message End
items.desc: Ends an original or adapted message.

items.label: Data Use Mine
items.desc: Carries application data as payload.

items.label: Data Use Yours
items.desc: Tells the processor to use kept original data.

items.label: Data Preservation Interest
items.desc: Says which original data may be reused.

items.label: Want Stop Receiving Data
items.desc: Server asks to stop getting original data.

items.label: Want Stop Sending Data
items.desc: Server asks permission to stop sending adapted data.

items.label: Stop Sending Data
items.desc: Processor grants that permission.

items.label: Want Data Paused
items.desc: Asks the peer to pause its data.

items.label: Paused My Data
items.desc: Confirms that data is paused.

items.label: Want More Data
items.desc: Asks for more data, ending a pause.

items.label: Negotiation Offer
items.desc: Offers a list of features.

items.label: Negotiation Response
items.desc: Accepts one feature or rejects the offer.

items.label: Ability Query
items.desc: Asks whether a feature is supported, without changing anything.

items.label: Ability Answer
items.desc: Answers an ability query.

items.label: Progress Query
items.desc: Asks for the peer's progress.

items.label: Progress Answer
items.desc: Answers a progress query.

items.label: Progress Report
items.desc: Unsolicited progress report.
